subject: ela
description: Students engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 6 topics, texts, and issues. They come to discussions prepared, having read or studied the material, and draw on that preparation by referring to evidence on the topic. They follow agreed-upon rules and roles for collegial discussions. They pose and respond to questions that connect ideas and contribute to the discussion. They build on others' ideas and express their own ideas clearly, and they review the key ideas expressed, demonstrating understanding of multiple perspectives. Because this is a speaking and listening standard, every item embeds the full discussion excerpt, transcript, sentence stem, or short stimulus it depends on, so the student needs nothing external to answer. Items assess the reasoning and language of good discussion rather than live performance: students evaluate, complete, revise, or analyze written transcripts and turns of talk.
subSkills: Come prepared: identify how a discussant has read or studied material and refers to evidence and textual details to support a point
Follow collegial rules and roles: recognize and apply agreed-upon norms (taking turns, staying on topic, listening, designated roles like summarizer or questioner)
Pose and respond to questions: ask questions that connect ideas and invite elaboration, and respond directly and relevantly to a question raised
Build on others' ideas: extend, agree with new evidence, respectfully disagree, or synthesize a peer's contribution rather than restating or ignoring it
Express own ideas clearly: state a claim or opinion with a reason or evidence in clear, complete language
Review and reflect: summarize key ideas expressed in a discussion and demonstrate understanding of multiple perspectives represented

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the building-on response
problemArchetypes.example: Read this exchange: 'JAMAL: I think the town should keep the old library open because it is the only quiet place to study. / PRIYA: ____' Which of Priya's replies best builds on Jamal's idea? Answer: 'That is a good point, and it also gives younger kids a free place to read after school,' because it adds a new reason that extends Jamal's claim instead of changing the subject or simply repeating it.

problemArchetypes.name: Choose the question that moves the discussion forward
problemArchetypes.example: Read the turn: 'LEO: The article says recess helps students focus, but it never explains how.' Which question best connects ideas and invites elaboration? Answer: 'What evidence from the article could help us figure out why focus improves?' because it builds on Leo's observation and asks the group to dig into the text rather than ending the conversation.

problemArchetypes.name: Apply a discussion rule or role
problemArchetypes.example: Read the norm and the situation: 'The group agreed that everyone must reference the text before giving an opinion. MAYA says: "I just think the ending is sad."' What should Maya do to follow the agreed-upon rule? Answer: She should point to a specific detail from the text, such as a line showing the character alone, before stating her opinion.

problemArchetypes.name: Spot the off-track or unhelpful turn
problemArchetypes.example: Read the discussion: 'TOPIC: Should the cafeteria offer more vegetarian meals? / SAM: Many students do not eat meat, so more options would include them. / DEV: My cousin plays on the soccer team.' Which speaker did not contribute effectively to the discussion, and why? Answer: Dev, because the comment is off topic and does not build on Sam's idea or refer to the issue being discussed.

problemArchetypes.name: Summarize key ideas and perspectives
problemArchetypes.example: Read this group discussion about whether students should grade their own homework, then choose the summary that best reviews the key ideas and shows understanding of multiple perspectives. Answer: the option that names both the view that self-grading builds responsibility and the opposing view that it could be unfair, rather than an option that reports only one side.

problemArchetypes.name: Revise an unclear contribution
problemArchetypes.example: Read the turn: 'TARA: It is just bad, you know?' Choose the revision that expresses Tara's idea most clearly for a discussion. Answer: 'I think the plan is unfair because it gives extra recess only to the older grades,' because it states a clear claim with a reason instead of a vague reaction.

Easy.description: A very short stimulus of two or three turns of dialogue (roughly 15 to 40 words total) embedded in the item. The task is to identify a single feature of good discussion: which reply is on topic, which speaker is listening, or which short question is relevant. The correct answer is obvious and only one discussion concept is tested. No inference about hidden meaning is required.
constraints: Stimulus is two or three short dialogue turns included in the prompt
Tests exactly one concept (on-topic reply, relevant question, following one rule, or clear vs unclear statement)
Identify-level task: pick the better turn or name what a speaker did
The supporting evidence is stated plainly in the dialogue, no inference needed

Medium.description: A short multi-speaker exchange (roughly four to six turns, 40 to 90 words) embedded in the item. The task requires analysis: choosing the reply that genuinely builds on a peer's idea versus one that merely repeats or contradicts it, selecting a question that connects two contributions, or identifying which agreed-upon rule a speaker followed or broke. The student must weigh several plausible turns, not just spot an obvious error.
constraints: Stimulus is a four to six turn exchange among two or three speakers in the prompt
Tests building on ideas, posing connecting questions, or applying a stated norm or role
Analyze-level task: compare turns and justify which one contributes effectively
Distractors are turns that are on topic but do not build, connect, or use evidence

Hard.description: A fuller discussion transcript (roughly seven to twelve turns, 90 to 160 words) among three or more speakers, embedded in the item, often on a grade 6 issue with competing viewpoints. The task requires evaluation and synthesis: choosing the summary that fairly reviews key ideas and multiple perspectives, judging which contribution best advances the group's reasoning with evidence, or deciding what a discussant should say next to integrate differing views. Requires inference about each speaker's stance and how the ideas relate.
constraints: Stimulus is a seven to twelve turn transcript with three or more speakers in the prompt
Contains competing perspectives or evidence that must be weighed
Evaluate or synthesize level task: best summary of multiple perspectives, best evidence-based contribution, or best next move
Requires inference about speakers' positions and how contributions connect

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student thinks restating or agreeing with a peer in different words counts as building on the idea
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a reply that simply repeats the previous speaker's point ('Yeah, I agree, it is the only quiet place') as the best example of building on an idea, instead of one that adds a new reason or evidence

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats any on-topic comment as a strong contribution, even when it does not connect to what others said
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses a turn that mentions the topic but ignores the previous speaker entirely as the response that 'builds on others' ideas'

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student believes the best discussion move is to state a stronger personal opinion rather than ask a question that involves the group
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Picks a turn that overrides others with a louder claim instead of the question that connects ideas and invites elaboration

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses giving an unsupported opinion with referring to evidence from the text or topic
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Accepts 'I just feel like it is wrong' as following a rule to use textual evidence, instead of a turn that points to a specific detail

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student summarizes only the viewpoint they personally agree with and ignores other perspectives in the discussion
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses a summary that reports one side of the issue as 'reviewing the key ideas,' leaving out the opposing perspective other speakers raised

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student thinks disagreement is always rude or off track and so cannot count as effective participation
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Labels a respectful, evidence-based disagreement as the speaker who did not contribute effectively, instead of recognizing it as a valid build on the discussion

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student values following a procedural rule (like turn-taking) over the substance of connecting and extending ideas
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a turn that takes a turn politely but says nothing relevant as the most effective contribution, over a turn that advances the group's reasoning
